title: Introduction
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how people work in many industries. It helps companies do tasks faster and make better decisions, but it also affects how much people get paid. Some jobs, especially those that involve technology or data, are becoming more valuable and may pay more. Other jobs may not see the same increase. This makes it important to understand who is benefiting the most from AI and how salaries are changing across different fields.
This topic matters because of emerging trends of companies starting to use AI, which is increasing the demand for certain skills. As a result, people with those skills may earn higher salaries, while others may not see as much growth. In this analysis, it is expected that jobs related to technology, data, and finance will see higher pay increases, while more routine jobs may not. Overall, AI is likely creating bigger differences in pay between different types of work (Brynjolfsson and McAfee (2014)).

title: Literature Review
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a force shaping modern labor markets in real-time. The expansion of generative AI technologies has accelerated changes in how work is performed, which skills are valued, and how compensation is distributed across occupations. Our research suggests that AI does not affect all workers equally. Instead, its impact varies significantly depending on the nature of job tasks, the level of worker skill, and the degree to which occupations can integrate AI. As a result, AI has the potential to both increase productivity and reshape wage distributions across disciplines. Understanding these dynamics is critical for evaluating how AI may influence salary disparities across industries and geographic regions.
Recent academic literature highlights that the relationship between AI and wages is complex and evolving. (Georgieff (2024)) finds that earlier forms of AI did not significantly increase wage inequality between occupations, although this evidence predates the widespread adoption of generative AI. Other studies suggest that the current wave of AI adoption may have stronger and more differentiated effects across the labor market.
For example, (Hartley et al. (2024)) shows that gen AI usage is more prevalent among higher-income, more educated workers, indicating that those already positioned in knowledge-intensive roles may be more likely to benefit from AI adoption. At the same time, (Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond (2025)) provides evidence that AI can significantly increase worker productivity—particularly among less experienced employees—and (Engberg et al. (2025)) suggests that AI may also help narrow performance gaps within certain occupations.
Further research emphasizes that AI’s impact extends beyond wages. (Engberg et al. (2025)) find that AI exposure is positively associated with wages at the worker level, but that these effects vary by occupation and skill composition. Meanwhile, (Frank, Ahn, and Moro (2025)) argue that traditional labor market indicators such as wages and employment levels may not fully capture AI-driven disruption, as some occupations face increasing instability even if wages remain stable.
The literature suggests that AI is likely to amplify differences between workers who can effectively leverage the technology and those whose tasks are more easily automated. This makes it important to examine salary disparities across disciplines, as well as differences between AI-related and non-AI-related roles, geographic regions, and work arrangements such as remote versus in-person employment.
This study seeks to analyze how AI is influencing salary outcomes across occupations and industries, with a focus on identifying which groups benefit most from its adoption and whether existing inequalities are being reinforced or reduced.

title: Analysis
text:
This section will present data analysis and findings on salary disparities across disciplines.
#data cleaning
We removed columns that do not contribute to the analysis, such as identifiers (ID), URLs, and tracking fields. These variables do not provide meaningful information for understanding salary patterns.
We also removed older versions of NAICS and SOC classification codes while keeping the most recent versions (NAICS_2022_6 and SOC_2021_4). This avoids redundancy and ensures consistency in how industries and occupations are represented.
This approach simplifies the dataset while preserving the key variables needed for analyzing salaries, job types, and industry differences.

Rows: 72498

This dataset contains job posting information that can be used to study salary trends, hiring patterns, and work arrangements. Before analysis, we inspected the number of rows and columns and reviewed the variable names to understand what cleaning would be needed.

title: Data Analysis
text:
2 Drop Unnecessary Columns
We removed tracking fields and redundant classification variables where present so that the dataset is easier to interpret and use for analysis.

columns_to_drop = [
    "ID", "URL", "ACTIVE_URLS", "DUPLICATES", "LAST_UPDATED_TIMESTAMP",
    "NAICS2", "NAICS3", "NAICS4", "NAICS5", "NAICS6",
    "SOC_2", "SOC_3", "SOC_5"
]

df_clean = df.drop(*[c for c in columns_to_drop if c in df.columns])

print("Columns before:", len(df.columns))
print("Columns after:", len(df_clean.columns))

Columns before: 131
Columns after: 118


We examined missing values to better understand data quality. Since our analysis focuses on salary, industry, and work arrangements, we kept only observations with usable values in key variables.

title: Data Analysis
text:
3 Handle Missing Values

df_clean = df_clean.filter(
    (col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull() | col("SALARY_TO").isNotNull()) &
    col("TITLE").isNotNull() &
    col("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").isNotNull() &
    col("NAICS_2022_6_NAME").isNotNull() &
    col("STATE_NAME").isNotNull()
)

print("Rows after filtering:", df_clean.count())

Rows after filtering: 32398


We examined missing values to better understand data quality. Since our analysis focuses on salary, industry, and work arrangements, we kept only observations with usable values in key variables. This approach preserves meaningful observations while ensuring that key variables are available for analysis. This filtering step significantly reduced the dataset size, indicating that many job postings were missing key salary or classification information. While this reduces sample size, it improves the reliability of our analysis by focusing only on complete and usable observations.

We converted posting dates to a date format so that date fields would be interpreted correctly.

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn(

title: Data Analysis
text:
5 Remove Duplicates

before_rows = df_clean.count()

df_clean = df_clean.dropDuplicates()

after_rows = df_clean.count()

print("Rows before removing duplicates:", before_rows)
print("Rows after removing duplicates:", after_rows)
print("Duplicates removed:", before_rows - after_rows)

Rows before removing duplicates: 32398
Rows after removing duplicates: 32398
Duplicates removed: 0


Duplicate job postings can inflate counts and distort patterns. To prevent double counting, we removed duplicate rows. No duplicate rows were identified in the dataset after filtering, suggesting that each job posting is already uniquely represented

title: Data Analysis
text:
6 Create Salary Measure
We created a midpoint salary using the lower and upper salary bounds to produce a single value for analysis. If only one salary bound was available, that value was used as an approximation so that we could retain more usable observations.

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn("SALARY_FROM", col("SALARY_FROM").cast("double"))
df_clean = df_clean.withColumn("SALARY_TO", col("SALARY_TO").cast("double"))

df_clean = df_clean.withColumn(
    "salary_midpoint",
    when(
        col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull() & col("SALARY_TO").isNotNull(),
        (col("SALARY_FROM") + col("SALARY_TO")) / 2
    ).when(
        col("SALARY_FROM").isNotNull(),
        col("SALARY_FROM")
    ).otherwise(
        col("SALARY_TO")
    )
)

df_clean = df_clean.filter(
    col("salary_midpoint").isNotNull() & (col("salary_midpoint") > 0)
)

df_clean.select("SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO", "salary_midpoint").show(5)

+-----------+---------+---------------+
|SALARY_FROM|SALARY_TO|salary_midpoint|
+-----------+---------+---------------+
|    62400.0|  83200.0|        72800.0|
|   169184.0| 217523.0|       193353.5|
|    74000.0| 118200.0|        96100.0|
|    87500.0| 158500.0|       123000.0|
|    95000.0| 100000.0|        97500.0|
+-----------+---------+---------------+
only showing top 5 rows


Instead of removing all observations with partial salary data, we constructed a salary midpoint using available values. If only one bound was present, that value was used as an approximation. This approach preserves more data while maintaining meaningful salary estimates.

title: Data Analysis
text:
8 Key Findings
The data cleaning process improved the usability of the dataset by removing redundant columns, handling missing values, converting date fields, and eliminating duplicate records. The exploratory analysis suggests that job postings are concentrated in a limited number of industries and that salary levels vary meaningfully across the sample. Remote and hybrid roles represent an important share of postings, which may influence how students approach their job search. The AI versus non-AI comparison is especially relevant to our project because it helps evaluate whether AI-related skills are associated with different compensation patterns.
